The experiments conducted on three diverse datasets (Text, Images, and Videos) show that our proposed method outperforms existing methods in achieving strong Top-K performance.

Theorized in 2008, quantum conduits facilitate the exchange of quantum information through time-irreversible channels. Unconventional to traditional systems, which exhibit Markovian behavior, these non-unical non-Markovian conduits display a distinct, enduring non-Markovian character. A newly proposed, analytical criterion for a quantum conduit to remain non-Markovian has been formulated, demonstrating its applicability in various instances. This method also allows us to identify a set of conduits that remain non-Markovian for an infinite duration, along with a few examples that last indefinitely in this non-Markovian state.

Deep learning models have excelled in image categorization, but their performance is limited by the scarcity of large-scale labeled datasets. To address this challenge, our proposed Active Categorization Framework (ACF) optimally utilizes limited resources to categorize images efficiently. ACF achieves this by leveraging active learning, which selectively queries annotator feedback. The framework relies on a novel counterfactual loss function (CFL) that, by comparing contrasting features, reduces the need for manual annotations. CFL also serves as a module for the ACF, which is trained iteratively through a process that involves sampling, querying, and refining. Our proposed method outperforms conventional active learning approaches by effectively optimizing queries with an uncertainty sampling strategy, demonstrating superior performance in comparison to existing techniques.

Robotic systems heavily rely on environment modeling for effective navigation. 
The complexity of real-world environments often hampers evaluation of new methods, 
as their applicability is unclear. 
Robotic simulation offers an efficient way to assess methods, 
but the scarcity of suitable tools and platforms hampers progress. 
Robotic Systems for Embedded Ecosystems (RoSmEEry) is a simulation platform 
designed to facilitate research in semantic mapping, 
featuring high-fidelity 3D environments replicating real-world settings, 
complete with accurate sensor data and labels. 
RoSmEEry is open-source and features a user-friendly web-based interface, 
enabling seamless integration of new methods via Python plugins. 
The platform's modularity and customizable content facilitate research in 
unrepresented or hard-to-reach real-world environments, 
enabling researchers to tackle complex challenges with confidence. 
RoSmEEry is available at https://rosmeery.icsi.iu.

Rikudo is a Japanese board game first introduced in 2014. It involves strategic planning and management of resources. Players take control of a group of warriors as they battle for dominance over a territory with multiple settlements. The ultimate goal is for one player to claim all settlements. Each turn consists of two phases: a phase for movement and a phase for action. A novel approach is demonstrated in solving Rikudo, proving it to be complex enough to require a specific method of analysis.

We propose a method for solving extensive optimal transport (EOT) by reformulating the problem into a multi-marginal optimal transport problem with a specific additional condition. This transformation allows the EOT problem to be solved using a modified Kantorovich duality, which can be approximated through a series of linear programs. A gradient ascent approach can be used to find an initial solution, after which a second family of algorithms can be employed to precisely determine the optimal transport plan. We suggest two specific algorithms, which can be chosen based on the specific requirements of a problem: Pregal, a fast and efficient method suitable for large samples size, and Exteo, a precise algorithm tailored for small samples.

Ramanujan's paper from 1913, which contains his famous modular identities, has been further expanded upon with various generalizations. We've taken it a step further by creating a "Hecke collection" that includes our own distinct identity.

We have obtained high-resolution infrared spectra of eight lensed quasars using the W.M. Keck 10-m telescope. Our analysis, carried out with the help of advanced data reduction techniques, has allowed us to pinpoint the emission lines of the lensing galaxies in each system, thereby enabling us to determine their redshifts with great precision. Furthermore, we have been able to measure the rotational speeds of the lensing galaxies with an accuracy of one percent, yielding estimated velocity dispersions ranging from 37 to 187 km/s. Our findings are consistent with previous estimates derived from photometric data, yet reveal notable discrepancies in a few systems. Notably, these discrepancies may be attributed to the presence of dark matter subhalos or the influence of internal star formation within the lensing galaxies. Our results will soon be integrated into the \textsc{graziers} gravitational lensing code, which simulates the distortion of light in gravitational lens systems.

This paper introduces a novel method for solving all types of q-fractional differential equations within time scales. We begin by examining the equivalent equation of a given q-fractional differential equation after a consistent time scale change, then map the solution of the original equation to the transformed problem, thereby providing a solution. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of this approach by solving q-fractional boundary value problems.

The phonon Hall effect presents an intriguing phenomenon where the plasmon Hall effect has been studied within a broader electromagnetic context. We employ a topological framework to examine the phonon Hall effect, leveraging an effective 2+1-dimensional acoustic medium with a dynamic structure resembling that of a quantum Hall system. In this model, an external magnetic field is simulated by an external vector vortex (or whirlpool) and a scalar protonical charge density. We derive an effective Hamiltonian that corresponds to a harmonic oscillator with a modified frequency and introduce an artificial harmonic potential to confine phonons within a finite area. This setup results in the formation of localized states, or 'islands', which are topologically distinct and give rise to distinct index values. Furthermore, these index values dictate the phonon Hall effect's behavior under time reversal and charge parity transformations.

Raman signals are typically too weak to distinguish from each other in broad field imaging, which is why image correlation is employed in SERDS microscopy to separate them. However, this method's accuracy is limited by the microscope's pixel resolution and number of pixels available for analysis. To improve this, we adapted the SERDS approach for use with Nod and Shuffle microscopy, which reduces the required number of measurements by utilizing a filter changer to substitute for spatial sampling. Our approach involves acquiring a single background measurement, then two sample measurements with the filter in different positions, and finally, subtracting the background from each sample measurement with the filter shifted. This results in two measurements that are subtracted in space rather than time, and our results demonstrate its effectiveness for analyzing biological samples and detecting single fluorescent molecules.

This paper explores matrix analogs of Fejér and Levin-Stečkin inequalities. We examine a specific type of matrix defined by a positive semi-definite operator on a Hilbert space, which maps an orthonormal basis to a bounded orthonormal set. We define this matrix by its action on this basis and assume its entries are symmetric with respect to the basis. We derive sharp inequalities for self-adjoint matrices meeting these criteria, which generalize the Fejér inequality and Levin-Stečkin inequality for finite-dimensional matrices. Furthermore, we extend these results to a subset of infinite-dimensional matrices, which includes Toeplitz matrices with a positive semi-definite and Hermitian off-diagonal part.

We examine the mean null energy condition for both Schwarzschild and Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker black holes that are experiencing evaporation.  Initially, we calculate the mean null curvature coupling in the context of holographic evaporating black holes.  Subsequently, we investigate the mean null energy condition for both types of black holes.  In the holographic case, we find that the mean null energy condition is violated once the evaporation process reaches a certain point, which is determined by the evaporation rate and the distance from the event horizon.  In contrast, we discover that the mean null energy condition holds true in the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker scenario, yet the average null energy density becomes negative once the evaporation process surpasses a critical point.  Notably, we observe that both types of black holes share a similar mean null energy density, which implies that both may collapse under similar evaporation conditions.  In the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker scenario, we determine the evaporation rate threshold beyond which the mean null energy density becomes negative.  In both contexts, we find that the evaporation process is restricted by holographic and geodesic localised information constraints.  In the holographic case, we find that the evaporation rate threshold aligns with the point at which the mean null energy density becomes negative.  In contrast, we discover that the evaporation rate threshold in the Friedmann-L

Note: This is an educational resource for students.
This note serves as a self-contained introduction to key conformal field theory (CFT) concepts, primarily focusing on the irreducible local field theory operators in a quantum field theory framework applicable across spacetime dimensions two and four, leaving a detailed analysis of other topics for further study.

Recent attacks on global industrial infrastructure have highlighted the need for improved cybersecurity. As a result, there has been increased focus on analyzing and evaluating cybersecurity for industrial control systems. However, existing research frameworks primarily focus on specific S&T challenges or assess cyber resilience through non-adaptive approaches. This study presents a comprehensive, adaptive evaluation framework called ICS-CTM2, which addresses the lack of suitable research frameworks for assessing ICS security. The proposed approach extends and refines an existing model called ICS-CTM, integrating a comprehensive methodology for assessing cyber resilience that adheres to ISO 31040 standards. The effectiveness of ICS-CTM2 is demonstrated through its application in a real-world scenario involving a water treatment plant's ICS system.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning presents a significant challenge of coordinating agents' actions to achieve desired outcomes, but current methods often rely on unverifiable assumptions and lack clear value estimation.  A new approach, the avericious approach, offers a more reliable foundation by incorporating individual value metrics into its framework.  By introducing ideal value functions to guide decision-making and employing the average of individual value metrics, the avericious approach provides a more robust multi-agent reinforcement learning method.  We validate the effectiveness of this approach by testing it in various environments with multiple agents, and the results demonstrate that the avericious approach outperforms previous methods in achieving optimal outcomes.

Current standards for measuring stereotypical prejudice in language models only assess unidirectional inference, whereas real-world implications involve bidirectional reasoning. We introduce StereoSet, a new benchmark designed to evaluate stereotypical prejudice in a two-way conversation. This involves developing a task that necessitates modeling downstream relationships using the pretrained language model's intermediate representations. The resulting StereoSet dataset consists of 1,500 pairs of statements and stereotypes from a range of sources across ten different demographic groups. We have conducted initial assessments using the BERT base model and observed that it exhibits a 60% likelihood of generating biased statements in response to neutral prompts from male speakers, whereas the bias is reduced to 42% when generated by female speakers. Furthermore, our findings reveal that BERT base models produce more stereotypical responses in the second utterance of a conversation compared to the first. We anticipate that future research will utilize StereoSet to evaluate and analyze the biases present in language models.

The focus of this work is on developing an efficient off-policy reinforcement learning approach for optimizing the electrical tilt states of a wind turbine's blades. The challenge lies in offshore wind turbines having a high upfront cost, making every component essential to minimize their operational expenses through enhanced energy production. The electrical tilt states directly influence wind turbine performance and, when inaccurately set, can lead to considerable energy losses. To address this, we created an off-policy reinforcement learning framework that enables learning tilt states without compromising wind turbine operation. The framework leverages existing knowledge from prior experience and demonstrates the value of off-policy reinforcement learning for the tilt optimization task. The results show that the learned tilt states can be successfully applied to wind turbines, resulting in a 2.5% increase in energy production compared to the default settings.

An assessment of the CKM angle gamma is conducted by combining the results from two LHCb experiments, one utilizing B+ to B- pi+ pi- pi+ pi- decays and the other B- to B- mu+ mu- and charged pi- or k- meson decays, in order to determine a more precise value of gamma. This updated analysis leads to a more accurate measurement, yielding a best estimate of gamma = (71.1 +/- 1.4) degrees. This is a significant improvement over the previous accuracy of and is in line with the Standard Model's predicted value. This new result is also in line with other existing constraints on gamma. This enhanced precision was achieved by utilizing two key advancements: a more precise calculation of the B+ to B- pi+ pi- pi+ pi- decay amplitude and a more precise determination of the B- to B- mu+ mu- and charged pi+ or k- meson decays' form factors.

This note addresses the classification of complicated ellipsoids, drawing on results from the theory of complex symmetry to identify distinct classes of second-order tensors. In conjunction with prior findings, it becomes evident that the complicated ellipsoids can be thoroughly characterized through their fundamental constituents.

The expansion of personal data markets has led to the development of new industries that exchange, analyze, and provide personal data-based services.  Yet, little is known about how the public views these emerging markets.  This study examines how laypeople perceive the trade of personal data and the motivations behind it.  We conducted an investigation of 104 community members and discovered that the majority do not explicitly object to the exchange of personal data for financial gain, although they may be concerned about the unauthorized trade of sensitive information.  However, our findings also reveal a desire to regulate the exchange of personal data in order to protect one's own information and safeguard society at large.  These results suggest that, in order to effectively govern the rapidly expanding personal data markets, researchers should consider collaborative approaches that incorporate both public and industry perspectives.

In the context of 16-QAM, faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling presents a complex problem of identifying transmitted symbols based on received signals. Traditional solutions, such as maximum likelihood (ML) decoding through sphere decoding, face significant challenges due to the emergence of new signal constellations in FTN signaling cases. To address this issue, this paper proposes a deep learning-driven ML decoding approach that leverages the similarities among FTN signaling cases to improve performance. By training a list decoding unit on a large dataset of known FTN cases, this method enables the identification of symbols with high efficiency. Simulation results confirm the efficacy of this approach for various FTN signaling schemes.

Impact algebras, a generalization of certain algebraic systems, serve as an alternative framework for utility theory. In this context, two topological structures are proposed for impact algebras: the order topology, derived from the impact algebra's natural impact order, and the Frink ideal topology, obtained by taking the closure of Frink ideals within the impact algebra's interior. Our analysis reveals that the order topology on impact algebras yields a compact space, with its interior being a lattice, while also being a Haar space. This space is found to be isomorphic to a superintuitionistic logic. Furthermore, the Frink ideal topology on impact algebras results in a compact Hausdorff space, with its interior being a distributive lattice, when the impact algebra is finite. Our discussion also touches on the conditions for the order and Frink topologies to be identical, with specific examples provided in both cases where they are not equivalent and when they are equivalent.

Recent advancements in deep learning models have achieved exceptional performance across diverse applications, yet these models often struggle with overfitting to training data noise and requiring sophisticated techniques like regularization to generalize effectively. To address this challenge, this paper presents a novel approach called SaliencyMix, which leverages object detection model outputs to identify regions of interest and apply random transformations or replacement, such as masking/scaling, to the input images for enhanced training signals. By incorporating SaliencyMix into supervised training, a significant boost in performance is observed on benchmark datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, with improved test accuracy even without model regularization.

We examine the trace of an operator on the infinite-dimensional Hecke algebra,
calculating its statistical moments in terms of Kostka numbers, and then
deriving formulas for corresponding moments in both types of algebras. In
affine A$_n$ cases, where the parameter is negative infinity, our results are
reconfirmed using a different approach. Furthermore, by analyzing the
asymptotic distribution within the limit of large algebras, we can see how the
Kostka numbers are related.

A novel method is proposed for examining gravitational theories by integrating intrinsic galactic alignments with cosmic shear. This approach involves using simulations to generate mock galaxy surveys, which are then analyzed for both intrinsic alignments and cosmic shear. By comparing the observed relationships between galaxy orientation and light distortion, it is possible to test alternative gravity theories. This work focuses on a simplified framework, which involves assuming a specific relationship between gravitational potential and light distortion. Our findings suggest that the proposed method can be used to constrain modified gravity models using current and future surveys, and provides a complementary method for testing these models.

In a state of suspension, the elastic response of the material to stress is influenced by the flexibility of its components. This study explores the dynamic relationship between stress and strain within a diverse system comprising soft particles that vary in terms of size, shape, elasticity, and responsiveness. By examining the time-dependent responses of the system to different stress applications, we observe a uniform viscoelastic behavior within the low-frequency range for all the systems examined. Conversely, their dynamic moduli reveal unique characteristics at higher frequencies, exhibiting a complex interplay between particle flexibility and size. Furthermore, the distinct responses of the system's rheological characteristics are attributed to the diverse characteristics of its constituent particles.

The formation of molten shells on gold nanoparticles is a crucial step in many photochemical processes, making their precise characterization essential for predicting their properties. We employ a machine learning-based approach, utilizing experimental data on the shape of molten gold nanoparticles provided by atomic resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), to develop a simulation tool. This tool enables us to model and extract information about the shape of molten gold nanoparticles from electron microscopy images. Notably, we find that the observed melting behavior in real-world experiments aligns with existing theoretical models, while our approach allows for a more accurate representation of this phenomenon based on the experimental data alone.

We provide parameterized theorems and bifurcation results for potential operators, which are either self-adjoint Hilbert space operators or differential operators within a specific function class. Our theory encompasses both finite-dimensional settings and infinite-dimensional frameworks. It encompasses Hermitian matrices, boundary value problems, and differential equations involving singularities or singular oscillations. We offer a comprehensive approach to bifurcation theory, covering local and global branch theories for both free problems and problems with constraints. We establish a general framework for proving our theory, which is based on applying the Krein-Rutman theorem to a parameterized operator that is closely related to the differential operator. We leverage this framework to discuss various aspects, including the Hopf bifurcation theorem, the Poincar\'e-Hilbert theorem, the Hopf-Andronov bifurcation theorem, the Hopf-Andronov-Hopf theorem, and others. We demonstrate how to extend these theorems to problems with constraints and provide examples of how these results can be applied.

The concept of taste involves a complex interplay of physical, biological, and psychological factors, despite the four traditional tastes being widely accepted. Recent research has introduced a broader 'tetrahedron of taste' model that acknowledges a distinct fifth taste, sweet, ultimately leading to a total of eight unique taste categories. A novel approach to understanding tastes involves utilizing a variational autoencoder to analyze descriptions of foods and their corresponding taste profiles. This method reveals that describing a food's taste resembles a process of mapping from a two-dimensional to a three-dimensional space within the tetrahedron of taste framework. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the second-order factor of this mapping can effectively represent the four traditional tastes, implying that only the third dimension is responsible for distinguishing the fifth sweet taste, and the remaining two dimensions govern the traditional tastes.

We derive expression of (h;q, α)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials as functions of (h; α)-Genocchi polynomials. New identities for (h; q, α)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials are formulated, and further extended to include (h; q, α)-stirling numbers and Bernstein polynomials with weight α. Moreover, the (h; q, α)-Genocchi polynomials and Bernoulli polynomials of the second kind are compared and analyzed in terms of their properties.

Long-term care costs pose a significant concern for policymakers, which is why analyzing the long-term impact of medical treatment is a crucial area of research. However, current methods for evaluating this effect are often limited by the length of available data, which can lead to significant bias if short-term and long-term patterns in treatment and outcomes are closely linked. In this study, we propose a novel machine learning method that can account for short-term and long-term patterns in treatment and outcomes, as well as the potential for long-term patterns to be influenced by various factors. Our simulation results demonstrate that this method provides more reliable estimates than existing approaches, including the Cox proportional hazards model and a model using state-of-the-art deep learning techniques.

To address how past events affect current or future health, causal inference methods are used in case-control studies. These events are often forgotten over time, which can be accounted for in data by using a model that shows how past events relate to current or future health. However, this approach doesn't consider how memories of past events might be influenced by current or future health. In the absence of data on how past events relate to current or future health, causal inferences based solely on a cohort study are made, which can lead to incorrect conclusions. This issue is particularly relevant in mental health research, where past traumatic events are often linked to current or long-term mental disorders. Our proposed framework addresses the challenge of how past events are distorted by current or future health and provides methods to calculate the impact of these events on current or future health.

Generative autoencoders, a type of model combining the capacity to encode and reconstruct data through inductive bias, have been increasingly utilized for generative and semi-supervised learning. Nonetheless, these models often fall short of achieving maximum likelihood training results due to data distribution discrepancies. To address this limitation, we've developed a novel training framework centered on utilizing invertible layers for data encoding. By leveraging the precise control offered by efficient encoding inversion, we've discovered a method to compute the likelihood's gradient and objective for training. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms conventional maximum likelihood training in a variety of datasets, data types, and applications including generative tasks and few-shot classification.

In today's rapidly evolving urban landscape, city administrators face a multitude of complex decisions daily to efficiently manage urban systems and provide citizens with the best possible services. The increasing availability of detailed urban data presents an opportunity for data-driven city management, yet city officials often struggle to transform this data into actionable insights. Our research goal is to create visual tools that help city officials assess the interconnections between urban features and create detailed scenarios for informed decision-making. By utilizing advanced visualization techniques, city officials can identify and analyze key relationships within massive datasets, ultimately enabling them to make data-driven choices that better serve the needs of the city.

This work explores the development of an optimal geometric multigrid preconditioner for a variety of HDG-P0 methods applied to reaction-diffusion and generalized Stokes equations. We establish a geometric multigrid preconditioner based on a V-cycle strategy and confirm that the associated preconditioned matrices exhibit spectral efficiency. This efficiency is demonstrated through the use of a multilevel decomposition technique combined with a norm equivalent to the HDG seminorm. We also propose an innovative V-cycle optimization strategy to enhance the condition number of the preconditioned matrices. Numerical results validate our theoretical findings and support the effectiveness of this approach for various coefficients and geometric configurations.

Missing data issues are prevalent in various fields, including medicine and economics, resulting from incomplete or unreliable collection of information. When a significant number of measurements are unavailable, or unreliable, the application of sensitive statistical methods without proper consideration can lead to biased conclusions. Sensitivity analysis aims to quantify this potential bias by estimating the range of outcomes that align with the obtained results under the assumption that the data were error-free. Bayesian statistics offer a systematic approach to sensitivity analysis, which is often applied in cases of missing data by utilizing an incomplete data model in conjunction with additional sensitivity models. We introduce the concept of the E-value, a proposed alternative to the causal graph sensitivity measure known as the S-ratio, which quantifies the Bayesian statistical evidence in a data-driven manner. The E-value is derived from the posterior predictive distribution of a target parameter, conditioned upon the primary parameter estimates and the assumed models. Through simulation-based experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of the E-value in various scenarios, including continuous, binary, and categorical data, and show that it can be effectively used to evaluate the reliability of findings in Bayesian missing data analyses.

A probability-based approach is proposed for assessing missing information in multivariate clinical trials where patients cross over to different treatment groups. This method allows for a more detailed understanding of losses in estimation accuracy due to missing data across multiple treatments. The application of this technique is shown through a simulation study examining its applicability in multivariate crossover trials, and its results are compared to those of a traditional efficiency loss approach.

This text focuses on categorizing and analyzing the categorial aspects of simplicial associahedra, specifically examining the conditions under which categories with "simplicial-like" structures are compatible and maintain a monoidal symmetry property.

DRAM is the primary memory technology in modern systems, but current DRAM chips lack the flexibility and customization options offered by other memory technologies. To address this limitation, researchers are developing innovative DRAM features such as phase change DRAM, persistent DRAM, and 3D-stacked DRAM. However, bringing these features to market is hindered by high development and production costs, making it challenging for DRAM manufacturers to adopt them and for users to deploy them. CODIC is a system that enables custom DRAM features and optimizations without modifying existing DRAM chips or DRAM controllers. It uses a custom DRAM substrate to integrate DRAM-related features such as DRAM debugging, DRAM profiling, 3D-stacking, and other memory technologies. CODIC is an affordable alternative to specialized DRAM chips, as it only requires a small number of expensive wafer-scale engineering chips to stack memory layers. CODIC is flexible and can be used to develop a wide range of DRAM-related features and optimizations, including DRAM security features, cache coherence protocols, memory-aware memory controllers, and more. CODIC is a modular system that can be used to develop and test DRAM features and optimizations in a cost-effective way.

This paper is the final installment in a series exploring the role of functional programming in the management and design of virtual network resources. It delves into the implications of network evolution and provides design principles for accommodating its complexities. By leveraging the De Bruijn's algebraic language, the study outlines fundamental rules governing virtual network transformations. Moreover, it examines the concept of network virtualization and proposes a model for its efficient design. Crucially, the research highlights the importance of a robust and scalable approach to network evolution, which is achieved through the integration of data processing and network resource management capabilities.

To explore the differences in multi-qubit gates and two-qubit gates within the toric code framework, an investigation of local and global gate operations is conducted. It is observed that a subset of a global gate ensemble can produce a range of local gate operations, and the minimum size of this subset is equivalent to the connectivity of the toric code. Furthermore, this study confirms that a more efficient subensemble exists, consisting of $4 \times 4$ local gate operations capable of generating the same set of two-qubit operations. In the context of quantum error correction, it is shown that a particular type of $4 \times 4$ local gate operation serves as a valid unitary transformation for the toric code states, and these gates are found to be more resilient to errors than their $2 \times 2$ local gate counterparts.

The OPUS system is a universal job management system that adheres to OPEER and POES standards, offering a comprehensive solution for processing complex tasks and service requests. By supporting these standards, OPES and OPEER enable efficient submission of parametric tasks and services to tera-scale resources, whereas POES facilitates the management of jobs and services in a standardized manner. OPUS provides a dual functionality - submitting jobs and services, as well as receiving and executing job broker and gateway services. As a web-based system, OPUS can be accessed via a web interface, enabling users to manage tasks and services with the Java-based OPUS Java API. The system leverages Java EE and JMS technologies, facilitating the management of concurrent tasks and services. As a result, OPUS is capable of processing an average of 100 submissions per minute, totaling 6,400 brokered submissions in a 24-hour period. The OPUS system is currently operational within the K computer project, specifically within the Astronomer's Grid, a collaborative Grid environment that encompasses various national and international institutions.

In today's technology-driven world, understanding and interpreting wireless network visualizations is essential for users to gauge the performance of their devices. This research focuses on creating an educational tool, called WiGEL, designed to teach individuals about complex wireless networks by utilizing digital game-enhanced learning. This innovative approach allows students to engage in a game-based simulation where they design and customize their own wireless network, guided by a comprehensive tutorial. Building on the findings from prior studies, we conducted an experiment involving 13 students and discovered that WiGEL's educational content effectively targeted both novice and intermediate-level students. Our results also indicate that the inclusion of wireless network visualizations within the game led to a positive learning experience, and we provide an analysis of the design requirements for effective game-based learning systems.

The widely used O3-O2 method for measuring O2's column density in planetary exospheres has been questioned by recent findings showing non-linear results in Earth's upper mesosphere. Despite this, the method remains widely used for exoplanetary characterization and atmospheric studies. To understand its limitations, we investigated the O3-O2 relationship across a wide range of atmospheric conditions, including those with varying O2 and O3 column densities, temperature profiles, and vertical mixing. Our results indicate that this non-linearity is widespread in Earth-like atmospheres and can significantly impact exoplanetary characterization. We found that using the O3-O2 method to determine O2's column density can result in errors exceeding 50% in some cases. Furthermore, the method's non-reversibility can lead to inaccurate O2 column density measurements, especially at high O3 concentrations. These findings highlight the need for more reliable methods for characterizing O2 in exoplanetary atmospheres and other celestial bodies.

We investigate non-equilibrium dynamics of a driven particle in the 3D quantum Hofstadter model. The dynamics of quasienergies in the Hofstadter model reveal two distinct flows along the edges of quasienergy bands in the bulk, which are topologically robust and persist in the presence of a strong magnetic field. These subdiffusive bulk flows are accompanied by ballistic surface dynamics. The surface flow is influenced by the quantum geometry of quasienergy bands and can be directed either towards or against the magnetic field. We demonstrate that the surface flow is intrinsically linked to the confinement of particles to quasienergy gaps and propose a method for manipulating the direction of surface flow through tailored driving of lattice sites.

Multilingual neural machine translation plays a vital role in breaking language barriers and facilitating communication in diverse settings, including healthcare. However, translating medical texts poses an added challenge due to the intricacy of medical terminology, making it essential to prioritize accurate medical information in translation. In response to this need, we introduce a domain-specific multilingual neural machine translation (MMT) framework tailored for medical domains and languages. The proposed MMT model leverages a domain-adaptation strategy, incorporating a novel loss function that emphasizes the preservation of medical entities and relations. Empirical evaluations on existing medical multilingual datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving notable improvements in translation quality and outperforming current state-of-the-art MMT models.

A theoretical investigation of the potential formation of both modified-ion-acoustic solitary and shock waves in a five-component plasma system has been conducted. This plasma system consists of warm positrons, warm electrons, a low-temperature electron population, and a balance of positive and negative ions. Using a fluid model for the ions and phase-space quantization for the electrons, the system was analyzed. It has been discovered that both types of waves can propagate in both directions in this plasma system under certain conditions. It was found that the background ion-temperature affects the propagation of waves differently and that the presence of warm positrons and low-temperature nonthermal electrons plays a significant role. Specifically, the presence of warm positrons stabilizes the waves while the low-temperature nonthermal electrons cause the propagation of the waves in a particular direction. This study highlights the importance of the low-temperature nonthermal electrons in the formation of both types of waves in a plasma system.

We introduce an unsupervised approach to pretrain multilingual dense retrieval models, which utilizes a sentence embedding model to generate contextualized vector representations. This is achieved through the application of a contrastive loss within a set of sentences, derived from varied sources including duplicate sets and tri-grams, which are then aggregated and processed in an unsupervised manner. Our pretraining method is evaluated across 11 languages and 3 public multilingual datasets for both dense retrieval and sentence embedding tasks, resulting in consistent top-ranked outcomes on all test datasets. Furthermore, through the lens of information retrieval, our pretraining method demonstrates enhanced performance compared to RoBERTa-based models, which in some cases, can only match performance by incorporating additional supervised training.

Multimodal learning, crucial for education, faces a significant challenge in effectively handling diverse data modalities. The issue is compounded by the fact that the availability of a particular modality can be unpredictable, leading to potential data imbalances. To address this, our proposed framework, PMR, employs a dual-attention mechanism to identify and mitigate data imbalance between modalities. The framework consists of a Prototypical Attention module and a Modal Rebalance module, which work in conjunction to minimize the disparity in information flow. The Prototypical Attention module assesses the similarity between modalities, while the Modal Rebalance module refines the representation by reducing inter-modality differences and maximizing intra-modality similarities. Through this dual-process approach, PMR achieves a balanced representation of multimodal data, as demonstrated by its application in the development of a system that scores the relevance of video comments to educational content. The effectiveness of PMR is further highlighted by its ability to improve model performance in low-resource modalities and to enhance model robustness in low-data scenarios.

Conveyance theory is an expanding area of study that focuses on how and when entities, such as animals, objects, and even information, are transferred or transported from one location to another. The movement of entities can occur through a single entity at once or, more commonly, through multiple entities working together to facilitate the transfer. The dynamic interaction between these entities influences both the efficiency and success of the transfer. The engagement between entities is crucial because it affects the effectiveness and even the possibility of transfer. This article aims to explore the principles governing the engagement between entities and their collective contribution to conveyance efficiency. We begin by examining the engagement properties of individual entities and their interactions in terms of cooperation, coordination, and integration. We then discuss how these engagement properties impact conveyance, presenting various engagement mechanisms and discussing the role of information exchange in conveyance success. Finally, we consider the potential implications of these findings for conveyance theory.

This study presents a novel end-to-end learning method that incorporates hybrid
combines of tensor-based models, combining the benefits of both tensor train
networks and truncated tensor networks. To accomplish this, the proposed
framework first employs a tensor train network to capture local patterns within
the input data, followed by the use of a truncated network to model the
temporal relationships within the input. Experimental evaluations were conducted
on two spoken command recognition tasks, demonstrating that our proposed
approach yields superior performance over traditional deep learning methods. 
Specifically, the proposed model achieved a significant 9.3% and 3.9% reduction
in word error rate when compared to conventional deep learning models on the
SCC-TDC and SCU-AILA benchmark datasets.

The breakdown of the population amplitude in a two-level system's density matrix generates the evolution of probability amplitudes for system states during a quantum measurement, defining the evolution as a quantum jump. This process is often interpreted as a real physical process, but its underlying physical interpretation is often ambiguous. This study shows that a broad range of distinct master equation forms can produce the same set of quantum jumps, indicating that multiple physical scenarios may be possible even if their dynamics are mathematically equivalent. We've identified a set of general master equations that can create any desired jump sequence and propose a criterion for physicality that constrains the system's dynamics, allowing us to distinguish between physical and unphysical evolution scenarios.

A novel approach utilizing plasmonic nanoparticles is applied to enhance the absorption capacity of silicon thin-film solar cells. Two types of plasmonic layers are examined: the first consisting of aluminum oxide nanoparticles embedded within a silicon layer, and the second with aluminum nanoparticles directly on top of the silicon layer. Both layers are subjected to and analyzed using same parameters and conditions. An investigation into the effect of varying nanoparticle shape on absorption enhancement is also conducted. Optical modeling techniques are utilized to study absorption improvements under varying light conditions, including monochromatic and angular incidence. The results indicate that the second configuration shows superior absorption enhancement, achieving up to 40% improvement, outperforming the first configuration. Furthermore, a study reveals that ellipsoidal nanoparticles yield the highest absorption enhancement among cuboid, spherical, and cylindrical shapes.

The concept of bounded query complexity refers to the ability to solve problems in less than exponential time on the size of input. This led to the development of bounded query complexity logic, which emulates polynomial-time computability without relying on enumeration constructs and quantification beyond existential limitations. However, previous attempts to build such a logic fell short due to the inability to incorporate universal quantification while maintaining bounded query complexity. This paper presents a novel bounded query complexity logic that overcomes this hurdle by introducing a selection operator and demonstrating its applicability through the creation of efficient algorithms for solving key problems, including reachability in unordered lists and determining strongly connected components in graphs.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have achieved top performance in various tasks, yet they come with a major drawback: their large memory requirements and high power consumption during training. To overcome this challenge, we present an innovative co-design strategy for energy-efficient neural networks that integrates data processing and hardware design to reduce power consumption. This approach leverages tensor decomposition to optimize the network's parameters, enabling significant reductions in size and complexity. By applying the Hierarchical Tucker decomposition method, we can efficiently break down large tensors into smaller ones that retain the original information and are more suitable for hardware implementation. We have developed an accelerated version of the HTD algorithm and a customized hardware accelerator based on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs). This customized hardware allows for efficient execution of the decomposed LSTMs while maintaining the same accuracy as the original models. Our results show that the proposed solution significantly outperforms other energy-saving methods, with a 2.7 times improvement in energy efficiency compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

The widespread adoption of drones in personal and commercial applications is largely attributed to the user-friendly control systems, known as GCS, which enable seamless interaction with the unmanned vehicles. These systems employ the MAVLink protocol, a well-established and widely used interface that facilitates real-time communication between GCS and UAVs. Notwithstanding its widespread adoption, MAVLink's security has received relatively little attention, with the majority of security audits confined to analyzing individual protocol messages, disregarding the inherent risks associated with the underlying protocol design. This paper presents MAVSEC, an innovative and non-invasive security solution that safeguards MAVLink communication, protecting against internal and external threats. MAVSEC incorporates a lightweight intrusion detection system that can be easily integrated into MAVLink protocol implementations, providing comprehensive protection against potential attacks. Our study demonstrates MAVSEC's effectiveness in detecting various types of threats, including spoofing, DoS, and attacks on MAVLink protocol implementation vulnerabilities.

The concept of (co)relational databases is gaining significant attention in the database research community. Relational databases are characterized by specific data storage properties, with a single value associated with each attribute. The presence of null values allows for relationships between independent facts, making it possible to reconstruct derived information. In contrast, co-relational databases are defined by multiple values stored as collections of tuples for each attribute. Although co-relational databases can represent a wide range of data types, they still fall short of capturing complex relationships found in real-world data, which often exhibit hierarchical and overlapping structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a new framework, Kollaps. This framework allows users to define a set of rules that describe the expected behavior of real data, even when individual facts do not conform to these rules. The Kollaps emulator, a crucial component of this framework, can be viewed as a co-relational database that applies user-defined transformations to individual facts to ensure they comply with the specified rules. The transformation rules can be dynamically added or removed by users to accommodate changing conditions.

The Newman-Penrose representation of asymptotically flat spacetimes can be derived from the complex phase space of Teukolsky space, which is a subset of twistor space and characterized by complex null geodesics. In doing so, the complex phase space can be partitioned into separate sectors based on the complex geometry of the Riemannian cone. The resulting representation of the Newman-Penrose map exhibits a natural breakdown into separate sectors within each null cone, which can be identified as the source and observer complex spaces of twistor theory. A key challenge within these sectors arises from complex self-adjointness, which necessitates a specific scaling of the Teukolsky operator. In contrast, the inhomogeneous sector of asymptotic Minkowski spacetime is characterized by a straightforward Lorentzian geometry, which can be leveraged to construct complex vector fields. A crucial aspect of the complex phase space representation lies in demonstrating that the complex phase space is homeomorphic to the Newman-Penrose map, which can be achieved through a detailed examination of the complex geometry within the cone.

Recent advancements in muon detector technology have made it feasible to utilize muons for subterranean imaging. A compact, gabbro-pesudocylindrical-simulating shape, GabbroPUC, was designed and modeled using Geant4. Anticipating future muon detector development on board a spacecraft, a space environment simulation was performed on GabbroPUC to assess radiation tolerance. Following space exposure, the detector demonstrated enhanced efficiency, with its muon detection capacity increased by nearly two-fold. Furthermore, the research evaluated the detector's resilience to heavy ions and resulting single-event effectiveness. Ultimately, the results of this study will inform the practical application of muon tomography for subterranean imaging.

A recent study introduced a new category of genetic algorithms inspired by nature, referred to as GLLAs. These algorithms are based on a specific operator that facilitates a random transformation of the search space. In the initial application, GLLAs were utilized to tackle the NP-complete Graph Coloring problem. The present research aims to extend this approach by integrating Parsing Expressions into GLLAs and applying them to tackle the challenging Vehicle Routing problem.

In this research, we examine how a previously discovered phenomenon, known as the Cherenkov vacuum radiation, occurs in the presence of a charged particle moving through a parallel electromagnetic field. The study focuses on the interaction of this particle with the fundamental symmetry of the electromagnetic field, specifically the U(1) U(1) symmetry. The investigation explores the implications of this symmetry on the radiation's properties, including the angle at which it is emitted and the radiation's energy. The study also considers the effects of temperature fluctuations, including the Planck distribution, on the radiation's behavior. Additionally, we derive the Boltzmann equations to analyze the behavior of the electromagnetic radiation within a plasma, taking into account the interactions between the particles and the radiation. The study also examines how the radiation's behavior changes when the particle's velocity approaches the speed of light in a vacuum, as well as the behavior of the radiation's energy at different temperatures and densities.

To gauge the accuracy of human predictions, we utilize a unique approach called forecast sampling, which enables us to track the evolution of perceived likelihood over time. By applying this method, we examined how people perceive the likelihood of upcoming words in a scripted scene from the TV show 'Parks and Recreation'. Our research found a notable disparity between the predictions of humans and those generated by BERT-based language models. Specifically, humans tend to make more consistent and flexible predictions, whereas BERT's predictions appear rigid and unpredictable. Additionally, we discovered that humans exhibit a capacity for adjusting their forecasts over time, a characteristic not seen in BERT's predictions. These findings suggest that human language processing involves a combination of both local and non-local influences, a claim we were able to verify using a BERT-based neural language model. Our research offers some potential explanations for these results, suggesting that human language processing is inherently more fluid and adaptable than that of current BERT-based models.

A novel approach to determine the three-dimensional position of an object from a single image is introduced, relying on the observation of its rotation. The method, called Unintentional Turntables (UT), leverages a neural network that can predict the three-dimensional pose of an object within a novel image, given its appearance in a training image. The approach is motivated by the common occurrence of objects rotating when interacting with other objects in everyday life. To optimize the method's efficiency, UT utilizes an innovative image-to-image translation framework that predicts an image from a given image, rather than requiring the re-computation of pose parameters. The approach is validated through both qualitative and quantitative analysis, showcasing its effectiveness on a variety of natural objects and scenarios. The UT method can be applied in multiple real-world scenarios, such as 3D reconstruction, object manipulation, and augmented reality.

The phenomenon of managed crossed Andreev reflection is observed in a hybrid structure comprising two quantum dots and an s-wave superconductor. By adjusting the gate voltages applied to the quantum dots, the transparency of M-CAR can be manipulated, enabling a significant change in current in nonlocal transport experiments. Furthermore, in certain systems with multiple Andreev bound states, EIT-like phenomena arise due to the phase lag between the phase of AR and the M-CAR process. To achieve an optimal phase lag, an optimal detuning is required, and this condition can be satisfied by adjusting the gate voltage of the superconducting lead.

A novel approach to the kinetic model of magnetic reconnection has been proposed. This approach incorporates an angle-of-attack scattering mechanism, allowing for an increase in particle energy up to values that are several times the thermal equilibrium value. A key aspect of our model involves the formation of reconnection current sheets, which exert a significant pressure gradient on particles through the Lorentz force. This pressure gradient causes a change in the angle of approach for the particles as they approach the reconnection X-point. Our kinetic model demonstrates that the angle-of-attack scattering resulting from this phenomenon can accelerate particles to significant energies, with some reaching values up to ten times the thermal equilibrium. This population of high-energy particles can contribute to the power-law tail in the particle energy spectrum observed in both laboratory experiments and space-based measurements.

The investigation of a theoretical model with an extended complex scalar sector is carried out by analyzing the Higgs and Z boson pair production at future electron-positron colliders. This model includes a light Higgs boson with possible non-standard interactions, as well as an extended scalar sector that can be used to address the fine-tuning issue in the Standard Model. The study examines the impact of new scalars on the Higgs coupling measurements, focusing on a scenario where the Higgs interacts with standard model fermions only through its SM interactions. The analysis of diphoton experiments at LHC, specifically the ATLAS and CMS, has been performed to constrain a possible non-standard diphoton coupling in this model. The results from this analysis have been used to constrain a theoretical parameter space in this model. The study also discusses the feasibility of precision Higgs pair production experiments at future electron-positron colliders to further constrain this model.

This paper aims to derive the subdifferential of the collective numerical radius for a broad category of bounded linear operators between complex Hilbert spaces. The underlying findings are strengthened by transference to a subdifferential rule governing the minimal off-diagonal perturbations of an arbitrary infinite matrix.

The growing use of the cloud has led to numerous applications, including big data analytics, machine learning, and internet of things, which heavily rely on cloud services.  However, ensuring the privacy of users' data in the cloud has become a significant concern. With the increasing amount of data being stored, ensuring user privacy has become a major issue. To address this problem, Differential Privacy provides a solution by applying randomness to protect sensitive information. However, the randomness used in the original DP frameworks results in significant noise that leads to a substantial loss of accuracy. To address this, research has focused on developing more efficient implementations that balance privacy and utility. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of the Monetary Vision-based Differential Privacy framework, which uses a new mechanism to improve the efficiency of DP. It also provides an evaluation of the framework's performance in different analytics tasks.

The concept of stochastic assignment in economic and social sciences is distinct from other types of optimization problems where variables are restricted to specific discrete sets.  In contrast, stochastic programming involves random variables whereas stochastic assignment allows individual constraints to define all possible outcomes.  This paper focuses on solving stochastic assignment and linear complementarity problems through a novel approach - random allocation fields and their associated Lagrangians.  These Lagrangians are derived from the correlation kernel, a matrix that represents the constraint set and plays a key role in determining the optimal solution.  The paper investigates the existence of random allocation fields and Lagrangians for various specific problems including the assignment, minimum cost flow, and bipartite matching problems.  In these cases, the optimal value of the Lagrangian can be interpreted as a measure of the stochastic potential - the minimum expected cost to reach a feasible solution from any feasible direction.  Furthermore, the optimal value of the correlation kernel or the stochastic potential can be calculated using well-known algorithms for these specific problems.  In particular, the stochastic potential for the minimum cost flow problem is given by the minimum cost to connect the origin and sink node in an unweighted graph, and for bipartite matching, it represents the maximum cardinality matching in an unweighted bipartite graph.

Research into laser-induced ignition of combustible gases with lasers has gained significant attention for its potential to significantly improve combustion systems' efficiency. This study investigates the use of high-powered, nanosecond lasers to initiate combustion in high-pressure, compressed He-H2-O2 mixtures and explores the effects of varying gas pressure, ignition energy levels, and optical focus size. The results show that a larger optical focus size allows for a wider range of conditions under which ignition is possible, with the optimal focus size being around 70 microns at a pressure of 50 bar. Furthermore, it was found that the critical energy required for ignition decreases as the gas pressure increases due to the larger available ignition area at higher pressures.

A novel network called the conformal boundary network (CBN) has been developed to produce high-quality segmentation results that are both accurate and efficient. CBN achieves this goal by creating a conformal transformation between two consecutive layers, allowing for the preservation of geometric properties. To further improve its performance, we introduced an additional network that can recognize and correct boundaries. This new network, referred to as the bR segmentation network (bRNet), utilizes a unique loss function and iterative process to generate and refine boundaries. Through extensive testing on various datasets, we demonstrated that the bRNet outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, especially when dealing with complex and noisy boundaries. Moreover, our implementation of the bRNet on a mobile device exhibits a high level of efficiency and efficacy in real-time online applications.

Modern driver assistance systems rely heavily on communication between vehicles to stay informed about their surroundings and nearby traffic. By pooling their information, vehicles can enhance the overall performance of vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) systems, leading to better traffic flow and reduced congestion. A key challenge in widespread V2V system adoption is determining the most effective method for data exchange and coordination among various road users, particularly in complex settings such as merging and diverging lanes. This paper proposes a collaborative driver messenger network that allows vehicles to relay information from distant sources, thus facilitating more efficient information exchange. We present a V2V communication algorithm tailored for lane merge scenarios, where a lead vehicle shares information with oncoming traffic using a messenger and the recipient vehicle shares this information with trailing traffic. Simulation results indicate that this novel approach can significantly reduce communication overhead while maintaining performance.

Using the approach of two-particle and large deviation theories, we examine how boundaries affect the distribution of non-interacting active particles moving in a channel. Our analysis focuses on a specific type of activity where particles can move faster or slower than diffusion, and we consider various scenarios including no, one, or two boundaries. We develop an exact solution for the steady-state distribution of particles and a simple approximation that accurately represents the distribution's key characteristics, such as its location, height, and width. Furthermore, we explore how these characteristics change with changes in certain physical parameters, and we also study the distribution of particles in different geometries, such as circular and rectangular shapes. Our results provide a framework to understand and predict the behavior of active particles moving in environments with boundaries.

The typical atom model, an approximation of a multi-photon process, is examined in this study, particularly in scenarios involving a short interaction time or weak coupling between the atom and the driving field. These conditions result in Siegert states, which are excitations with non-zero momentum that arise from the atom's initial state. The investigation focuses on the second harmonic generation process, where the atom's final state consists of a coherent superposition of energy states resulting from second-order transitions. The analysis reveals that the coherence of the resulting second harmonic is significantly influenced by the momentum of the atom, which introduces a critical factor that affects the efficiency of the process. Moreover, it is discovered that the typical atom model can produce a higher average energy flux than the Born-Markov model, provided the coupling strength is sufficiently low. The study also explores the impact of the atom's self-interaction potential, which can lead to the emission of unbound particles and affect the coherence of the emitted light.

Observations of the Si IV 1390-6 doublet in a solar flare were made using the IRIS satellite, showing rapid fluctuations in this narrow spectral line. The line strength varied significantly over very short periods, just a few seconds, during the flare's peak emission. The observed variations in line strength are consistent with changes in the plasma's temperature, suggesting extreme changes occur on a very small scale, possibly within a single resolution element. The rapid changes in line strength were not caused by changes in non-thermal velocity or opacity, suggesting that they are due to variations in the plasma's temperature. The data show that the Si IV 1390-6 emission is highly dynamic, appearing and disappearing in a matter of seconds, and this behavior is consistent with the plasma being in a non-equilibrium state, possibly a current sheet.

We explore the difference in behavior between the Peccei-Quinn mechanism and the QCD axion dark matter, based on the assumption that their origins are linked to distinct classes of couplings, specifically $\phi/\Lambda$. By incorporating a new variable, $r$, representing the difference in their behavior, we find that $r$ either has to be very small or the P-Q mechanism will fail. Using the electric dipole moment constraint, we place a limit of $|r|\lsim 10^{-4}$, implying that the P-Q mechanism will collapse if $r$ is not the dominant factor. This result further suggests that the difference in their origins may necessitate the existence of a new sector, potentially replacing QCD axions as the primary candidate for dark matter.

The impact of a post-irradiation annealing process on the material properties within the damage and undamaged regions is shown to influence nanopatterning in thin films. Specifically, this impact is examined through the use of two analytical models, which consider the lateral and axial physical processes occurring during the annealing process in the undamaged region and the evolution of the damage region, respectively. The former model is based on the established treatment of the damaged area as a source of excess point defects and is used to explain the increased solubility of impurities in the undamaged region. The latter model is based on the established concept of a damaged area diffusing into the undamaged region and is used to explain the increased solubility of impurities in the undamaged region. The results of these models are compared to experimental results obtained from the thin films irradiated by 40 MeV helium ions, which were then annealed at 400°C. The findings indicate that the undamaged region can absorb impurities from the damaged area, thereby affecting the solubility of impurities in the undamaged region and consequently altering the critical angle for nanopatterning.

Digital plagiarism detection techniques have been under research for decades, 
yet they face significant limitations when applied to object-oriented languages, 
specifically due to code translation, syntax differences, and object-oriented structures. 
This work introduces an implementation of an object-oriented code anti-copying system, 
leveraging navigation approach methods to protect source code against direct duplication. 
The developed framework is specifically designed for C# language applications, 
focusing on four key object-oriented elements - classes, methods, properties, and events. 
To enhance security, the anti-copying process integrates multiple techniques, 
including navigation sequence analysis, syntax modification, and randomized naming conventions. 
Furthermore, the evaluation incorporates metrics from information theory and data condensation, 
assessing the trade-offs between preserving navigation information and reducing unauthorized knowledge. 
The proposed system's efficacy is demonstrated through comprehensive experimental results.

We analyze the behavior of a specific type of series that involves the mean values of Dirichlet characters evaluated at prime powers, where the coefficients are weighted by the reciprocal of their absolute values. Under certain conditions, we demonstrate that this series is completely convergent for a wide range of integer parameters. In some instances, we further establish that the series is convergent in a particular sense known as L$^2$, implying the series is in fact convergent in the traditional sense. These findings have implications for the complete convergence of Dirichlet series, such as those resulting from the summation of mean values of Dirichlet characters and the values of certain types of automorphic L-functions.

We investigate the properties of a specific type of near-subgroups in groups with a metric, focusing on near-normal subgroups and their role in the group structure. The theory of metric geometry reveals that many group properties, including normality and the two-sided Green relation, can be expressed in terms of metric distances. This work explores how the distance between group elements can be used to characterize near-normal subgroups. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a metric on a group defines the distance between an element and its conjugate based on its distance to the identity element. Moreover, if a near-norm on a group is invariant under conjugation, then it defines both a near-norm and normality on the group, and the distance between elements in different conjugacy classes must be greater than or equal to twice the distance between the identity and any non-identity element within that class.

In statistical machine learning, a key challenge involves estimating a log-concave probability density function from sparse, unstructured data sets. This task is crucial for many applications, including topic modeling and Bayesian nonparametrics. Theoretical advances have established conditions for model convergence and effective sampling, but a practical method to achieve these results from finite data remains elusive. This paper develops an innovative estimation technique to tackle this issue by constructing a model that guarantees log-concavity, incorporating finite data support, and allowing practical constraints such as non-negativity. The proposed method exhibits desirable theoretical properties, including model selection and sparsity, and its practical effectiveness is demonstrated through comparison with state-of-the-art baselines on various synthetic and real-world data sets.

The static configurations of granular materials can be described by a point cloud representation. These configurations can be categorized into distinct types based on their overall shape. To efficiently categorize all configurations, we utilize the Wang-Landau algorithm to calculate the entropy of a system with fixed particles. By performing simulations with various initial conditions, we can accurately determine the entropy of a given configuration. Additionally, we propose a method to estimate the number of configurations with the same entropy level, which is useful for identifying and counting distinct microstates with the same index of state.

We introduce a new graph theory concept, known as the adventurer-manager game, where two players compete on a given graph. Player 1, the adventurer, starts with a designated starting node, and her goal is to find a sequence of neighboring nodes, while player 2, the manager, aims to slow down the adventurer and force her to take longer sequences of nodes. The manager can add a new node along an existing path, while the adventurer must continue without stopping. We define two metrics: the adventurer's cost is the number of nodes in her path, and her diameter is the minimum cost distance she can achieve. The manager's advantage is the maximum factor by which the adventurer's diameter may be increased without limit. Our research shows that on any graph, the adventurer's diameter is maximally optimized when her diameter equals the manager's advantage. We also provide examples and further results, including connections to other concepts in graph theory such as metric dimension and graph minors.

This study explores how the frequency associations in the spectral distribution of Gaussian processes (GPs) evolve over time, focusing on the common link between space and time. By analyzing the relationship between space-space and frequency-frequency correlations in GPs, we investigate how the spectral properties of natural phenomena can provide new insights into their behavior over time. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the spectral analysis of these correlations can help identify the type of temporal Gaussian process involved.

This paper's primary goal is to identify the one-dimensional potential $V(x)$ that enables stable soliton solutions for the Broer-Kaup system. To accomplish this, the Broer-Kaup system is converted into a novel integrable Hamiltonian equation set, along with its conjugate Lagrangian, allowing for the derivation of conservation laws based on Noether's theorem. By applying a variational calculus approach, the paper identifies and examines one-dimensional potentials $V(x)$ that yield long-term stable solutions and provides a list of potential candidates that support the existence of soliton-like structures.

We explore the existence of weak solutions to the incompressible Euler equations in ℝ³ that preserve energy over time. Our approach centers on the concept of the Helmholtz-Schmidt operator and its positive definite tensor, from which we derive the conservation of circulation for our solutions. Furthermore, through the relationship between the tensor and circulation, we establish that the continuous weak solutions, which lack regularity, can still conserve energy. Ultimately, we establish the existence of weak solutions with bounded circulation, thereby ensuring the long-term conservation of energy.

The VIRUP initiative is a collaborative project between CNES and Caltech, focusing on space and astronomy research and exploration through immersive virtual reality technology. Its key objectives include developing innovative VR experiences that make astronomy accessible to everyone, creating engaging educational content for schools, and producing entertaining VR games. Additionally, VIRUP aims to design and author immersive experiences for therapeutic and rehabilitation purposes, supporting users in simulating real-world situations and facilitating better understanding of complex issues such as anxiety disorders and blindness. Another significant goal of the initiative involves designing and authoring therapeutic applications for treatment and rehabilitation of individuals with dissociative disorders and those experiencing social anxiety. Finally, VIRUP seeks to create a platform for publishing and sharing VR experiences and to establish a community of authors and experts in the field.

The Data Bricks Cosmic Expedition is a hands-on project focused on teaching middle school students the significance of data. Through a game-based environment, students develop an understanding of data by designing and developing their own Earth-like planet. The long-term objective is to show students that, while they may not fully comprehend data, similar data-driven tools are instrumental in shaping science, engineering, technology, and mathematics disciplines. By collaborating with science teacher, Mrs. Kelli Ward from Houston Independent School District, we introduced this project to her 7th-grade students in two sessions. Using a data visualization tool, we created a virtual world where students could design and develop their own Earth-like planet. The results revealed that the project successfully conveyed the value of data and even sparked interest in space exploration.

A key aspect of Software Defined Networking (SDN) lies in its ability to manage and control the data-packed data-paths within the SDN-enabled network devices. Each data-path is unique, reflecting the specific traffic flowing through the network at a particular point in time, making it a crucial factor in SDN's performance. Identifying the characteristics of these data-paths is essential to optimize the network's operation effectively. In this research, a novel method is proposed to detect and analyze data-paths by examining the traffic patterns within the network, and a real-world implementation is demonstrated using the OpenFlow protocol.

Strong relational inference abilities are crucial for tasks requiring understanding complex scenes. Our research introduces Relational Intelligence, a new metric to gauge how well representations capture information about an image's underlying structure. We show that a strong relational foundation enables a model to effectively learn distinct factors of variation within an image, known as weak disentanglement. To demonstrate this, we developed the Synthetic Relational Dataset, a collection of images generated using a simulation, where real and simulated ground truth is accessible, allowing us to assess models' ability to learn image generation principles. We also created a new weakly-disentangled evaluation metric, based on the Simulated Image Captions dataset, to help identify relationships between image elements. We then developed a generative model, SemiAutoEncoderVAE, capable of producing accurate representations of scene graphs, and training it to generate images that capture the underlying structure. Finally, we used our framework to test top-performing models from prior research and found that they fail to adequately capture the image's relational and disentangled aspects.

A novel oscillating foil concept is being developed to improve WEC performance, leveraging synchronized movement of its components. The present study explores the interaction between the primary foil and its trailing attachment, focusing on the effects of the trailing foil's amplitude and phase delay on energy harvesting efficiency in different scenarios: the 'delayed' and 'opposite phase' cases. The theoretical model used in this study describes the complex wake created by the primary foil, taking into account the non-linear characteristics of the wake and a quadratic drag force related to the velocity gradient. The analysis considers various trailing foil amplitudes and phase delays, revealing that the 'delayed' scenario generally offers higher energy efficiency than the 'opposite phase' scenario. The study also examines the energy efficiency in both cases and identifies the optimal phase delay for the trailing foil.

We introduce a statistical method to determine the real-time dynamics of lattice QCD by analyzing thermal particle distributions. This approach enables us to accurately estimate real-time transition amplitudes with minimal human intervention, where the underlying principles are specified by a lattice QCD model. Our results show that this method can accurately reproduce the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics in complex systems, specifically the CPT theorem.
